title: Write-ahead logging and crash recovery
goal: By the end you can explain why a database logs every change before it changes a page, state the commit rule and the WAL rule, trace crash recovery from a checkpoint using page LSNs, say in plain words what ARIES's analysis, redo and undo passes do, and build a small store that survives a crash at any point.

warmup.q: A transaction updates two rows on two different pages of a PostgreSQL table, and COMMIT returns. What has reached the disk at that moment?
options: Both data pages, written and fsynced by COMMIT
Nothing yet: everything stays in shared_buffers until the next checkpoint
The WAL records for both changes and the commit, forced to disk, but neither data page
The two data pages, but not the WAL, which is written in the background
warmup.why: COMMIT forces the write-ahead log up to the commit record and returns. The data pages stay dirty in memory and are written later by the background writer or a checkpoint; the first Try it shows both pages still dirty after COMMIT. If nothing reached the disk, a crash would lose a committed transfer. The last option has it backwards: the log must be durable first.

sections.h: A commit forces the log and leaves the pages for later
sections.body:
Lesson 3's dirty pages and lesson 5's memtable share one weakness: they hold changes that exist only in memory until something writes them out. This lesson makes those changes survive a crash. Take a transfer of 25 euros between two wallets. It changes two rows on two different pages: page 0 and page 132 of the `accounts` table in the first Try it. Both changes must survive a crash, and they must survive together. A debit without its credit is money that vanished.

Version 1 writes both pages to the data file at COMMIT and forces them to disk. That is two 8 KB writes at two places in the file, plus a force that lesson 1 measured at about 4 ms on a laptop. And it isn't even safe. If the power fails after the first page is written and before the second, the disk holds the debit without the credit, and nothing says the transfer was half done.

Version 2 first copies the old contents of both pages to a separate journal file, then overwrites the pages. After a crash, a leftover journal means "put these pages back". That is SQLite's default rollback journal, and it is atomic. It still writes every changed page at commit, twice.

Version 3 is the **write-ahead log** (WAL). For every change, append a small record that describes it to one log file, the append-only kind from lesson 1: "on page 132, set the balance in row 14 to 102,500". Change the pages only in memory, in the buffer pool from lesson 3. At COMMIT, append a commit record and force the log. That is one sequential write and one fsync for the whole transaction, shared with any other transactions that commit at the same moment (group commit, lesson 1). The changed pages stay in memory, marked dirty, and reach the data file later, in the background. If the power fails first, the log holds everything needed to redo them. In the second Try it, a transfer writes 200 bytes of WAL. Writing its two pages would be 16 KB.

So a commit writes the log, not the data. Recovery papers call "pages are not written at commit" **no-force**, and "a dirty page may be written before its transaction commits" **steal**. PostgreSQL does both: the buffer pool may evict a page with uncommitted changes whenever it needs the frame. Your lab is simpler. It keeps a transaction's changes out of the pages until it commits.

The figure is the picture for this lesson. The log runs ahead and is forced at every commit. The data files lag behind, and they are allowed to, because the log can rebuild them.

try.title: Commit leaves the pages dirty
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Create `accounts` with 20,000 rows, find the pages of rows 42 and 17042, and run a CHECKPOINT so that no page is dirty.

Run a transfer between the two rows. Predict which pages are dirty after COMMIT, then compare page 0's LSN in memory with the LSN in the first 8 bytes of the data file. Run CHECKPOINT and read the file again.

sections.h: LSNs tell the database whether the log is ahead of a page
sections.body:
Two rules make the log trustworthy, and both need a way to compare a page with the log. That is the **LSN**, the log sequence number from lesson 1: a record's byte position in the log. PostgreSQL prints it as two hex numbers, like `0/2F12D5D8`. Two positions in the log matter: where the next record will go (`pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()`), and how far the log is durable, the flush LSN (`pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()`). Each page carries one more, the **page LSN**, in the first 8 bytes of the page header from lesson 2. It is the position just past the last log record that changed the page.

The commit rule: COMMIT returns only after the flush LSN has passed the commit record. That is what makes a commit durable.

The WAL rule, which gives the log its name: before a dirty page is written to the data file, the log must be durable at least up to that page's LSN. The log goes ahead of the data. Break the rule and a crash can leave a page on disk that holds a change the durable log never recorded. Recovery can't redo what it can't see, and it can't undo what it doesn't know about. In your lab, a transfer's debit page could reach the disk while its commit record is still in memory; one of the lab's tests stages exactly that crash.

In PostgreSQL the buffer manager enforces the rule. Before it writes a dirty buffer, it calls `XLogFlush` with the page's LSN, which flushes the log first if it has to. It rarely has to, since commits keep the log far ahead of the pages.

One setting relaxes the commit rule and keeps the WAL rule: `synchronous_commit = off`. COMMIT returns without waiting for the flush, and the WAL writer process flushes within at most three times `wal_writer_delay`, 600 ms by default. A crash can lose those last transactions entirely, but never half of one, because no page holding their changes can reach the disk ahead of their log records. The docs put the risk as "some recent allegedly-committed transactions being lost". For a payment a client was told is captured, leave it on.

The Try it reads one transfer's records with `pg_waldump` and finds each page's LSN equal to the end of the record that last changed it.

sections.h: Recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint
sections.body:
After a crash the data files are a mix. Some pages have every committed change, some are minutes behind, and the log holds the difference. Recovery reads the log and redoes what the pages are missing. Two questions decide how: where in the log to start, and how to tell whether a page already has a change.

Starting at the beginning of the log would work, but it could take hours, and the log would have to be kept forever. A **checkpoint** sets a limit. It writes every dirty page to the data files, fsyncs them, then logs a checkpoint record that names the redo point, where recovery may start. PostgreSQL keeps the location of the latest checkpoint in a small file, `global/pg_control`. Every change before the redo point is guaranteed to be in the data files, so recovery starts there, and older log files can be recycled. PostgreSQL checkpoints every 5 minutes (`checkpoint_timeout`) or sooner when about 1 GB of WAL has piled up (`max_wal_size`), and spreads the page writes over most of that time so they don't arrive as one burst.

The page LSN answers the second question. Recovery applies a change only if the page's LSN is below the position of the record. If the page reached disk after that change, its LSN already covers it, and the record is skipped. That makes redo **idempotent**: if the power fails again during recovery, the next recovery replays the same records and ends in the same state. The stepper runs a whole recovery.

What about transactions that never committed? Their records can be in the durable log, flushed by someone else's commit, like T2 in the stepper. In an engine that steals, their changes can be on disk pages too. Your lab never lets uncommitted changes into pages, so recovery just drops their records. Real engines follow ARIES, the recovery design IBM published in 1992. In plain words, it makes three passes over the log:

1. Analysis reads from the last checkpoint to the end of the log and works out which transactions were still open at the crash (the losers) and which pages may be missing changes.
2. Redo replays every change from the redo point, committed or not, wherever a page's LSN shows it is missing. ARIES calls this repeating history: afterwards the pages look exactly as they did at the moment of the crash.
3. Undo rolls the losers back, newest change first, using the undo information they logged. It logs each undo step too, as a compensation record, so a crash during recovery never undoes the same change twice.

InnoDB and Oracle follow this design. PostgreSQL repeats history from the redo point like ARIES, and has no undo pass at all. A transaction with no commit record counts as aborted, and every row version it wrote, stamped with its id in `t_xmin` as lesson 2 showed, is invisible to every query; the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC covers these visibility rules. In the Try it, the loser's row version is still on the page after recovery, and nobody can see it.

The log ends where its records stop checking out: at the first record that is short or fails its CRC, as in lesson 1. PostgreSQL logs that point as `invalid record length`.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: WAL configuration (checkpoints and the redo record)

sections.h: A half-written page needs a whole copy in the log
sections.body:
There is one crash that redo can't fix on its own. PostgreSQL writes 8 KB pages, but a drive only writes whole sectors of 512 bytes or 4 KB. If the power fails in the middle of a page write, the page on disk can be half new and half old: a **torn page**. A log record like "set the balance in row 14" assumes an intact page; replayed onto a torn one, it produces garbage. Data checksums, on by default for new clusters since PostgreSQL 18, detect a torn page but can't repair it.

InnoDB's answer is the doublewrite buffer: write each batch of dirty pages first to a separate doublewrite area, fsync it, and only then write the pages in place. After a crash, a torn page has an intact copy to restore from. The first write is one big sequential chunk with a single fsync, so it costs far less than writing everything twice. Facebook's MyRocks paper still names it as one reason InnoDB wrote so much to flash, the numbers lesson 5 compared.

PostgreSQL does it inside the log, with **full-page writes**. The first time a page changes after a checkpoint, the log record carries an image of the whole page, a full-page image (FPI). Recovery starts at a checkpoint, so the first record it finds for any page is that image: it restores the page from the image, torn or not, and replays the later small records on top. Further changes to the page before the next checkpoint log only the change.

You pay in log volume right after each checkpoint. In the Try it, 200 updates spread over 120 pages write 902 KB of WAL just after a checkpoint, and 21 KB when the same updates run again a moment later: 120 page images, then none. That is the real trade-off in checkpoint spacing. Frequent checkpoints mean a short recovery and more page images; rare ones mean less WAL and a longer recovery. `wal_compression` shrinks the images (LZ4 and Zstandard since PostgreSQL 15): the same burst wrote 303 KB with lz4.

Leave `full_page_writes` on. The docs allow turning it off only on a file system that prevents partial page writes itself, such as ZFS. And this is the reason lesson 1's append-only store never needed any of it: it never overwrites a page that holds live data.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Reliability (partial page writes, full page images)

analogy: A write-ahead log works like a chess game played by post. Each player keeps the list of moves in a notebook, and the board on the table is only a convenience. If someone knocks the board over, you set up the position from the last photo you took of it and replay the moves written after it; a move the board already shows is skipped. The photo is the checkpoint, the notebook is the log, and the rule that you write a move down before you touch the pieces is the WAL rule. The analogy breaks at unfinished moves: in chess every move written down counts, but a database log also holds records of transactions that never committed, and recovery must leave those out.
in_your_world: Oracle works the same way: at COMMIT the log writer (LGWR) writes your redo to the online redo log, and the database writer (DBWR) writes data blocks later; Oracle keeps undo in undo segments to roll back losers, as ARIES does. In PostgreSQL you can relax the commit rule per transaction with `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off` for writes you can afford to lose, such as an audit event or a metrics row, and keep it on for captures and ledger entries. Know what your other stores promise. A Cassandra node's default `commitlog_sync` is `periodic` with a 10-second period, so a single node acknowledges a write before its commit log is fsynced and relies on replicas for durability. And if you use Temporal, you already depend on this idea: a workflow's state is rebuilt after a worker crash by replaying its event history, a log of what happened, from the start.
mistake: The common mistake is turning off `fsync` (or `full_page_writes`) to speed up a bulk load or a test environment, and carrying that config into production. The server runs faster and nothing looks wrong until the first power loss or kernel crash, when the WAL rule no longer holds on disk and pages can be torn: PostgreSQL's docs warn that `fsync = off` can lead to unrecoverable corruption. People do it because benchmarks and CI get faster and every test passes. If you need speed and can lose the last few transactions, use `synchronous_commit = off`, which keeps the database consistent. For a one-off bulk load, use `COPY` and unlogged tables you can rebuild, then switch them to logged.

compare.title: After a crash, an uncommitted transaction: your lab vs PostgreSQL

a.label: Your lab
a.title: changes applied at commit
a.src:
while running:  UPDATE records are logged,
                pages are NOT changed

recovery:       collect UPDATEs per transaction
                at its COMMIT: apply them where
                  page LSN < commit end LSN
                no COMMIT: drop its records

undo needed:    never: no page held the change

b.label: PostgreSQL
b.title: changes applied at once
b.src:
while running:  each change is logged AND
                written into the page (in memory),
                the page may reach disk (steal)

recovery:       redo every record where
                  page LSN < record end LSN,
                  committed or not
                no COMMIT: transaction counts as aborted

undo needed:    none: MVCC hides the aborted
                row versions; VACUUM removes them

compare.note: Both are redo-only, for different reasons. Your lab never lets an uncommitted change into a page, which is simple but would mean holding every change of a long transaction in memory. PostgreSQL lets changes into pages immediately and relies on visibility: every row version carries the id of the transaction that wrote it, and a transaction with no commit record is aborted. ARIES-style engines such as InnoDB and Oracle choose a third way: redo everything, then run an undo pass with undo records.

Write `flushPage` (flush the log up to the page's LSN first: the WAL rule) and `checkpoint`.
Write `recover`: find the redo LSN through the control file, call `wal.recover`, collect UPDATEs per transaction and apply them at COMMIT where the page LSN is lower.
Run the tests until all 11 pass. If "log before data" fails, look at `flushPage` first.
hints: Stamp pages with the COMMIT record's `endLsn`, not an UPDATE's. Then the WAL rule in `flushPage` flushes the commit record before the page, which is what keeps a transfer all-or-nothing.
In `recover`, keep `HashMap<Int, LinkedHashMap<Int, Long>>` (transaction id to page to value), so a page written twice in one transaction ends with the last value, as `Tx.writes` does.

In `checkpoint`, the redo LSN is `active.values.minOfOrNull { it.firstLsn } ?: wal.nextLsn`. Flush the CHECKPOINT record before `control.write`, or a crash could leave the control file pointing at a record that isn't on disk.
Set `nextTxId` past every transaction id recovery sees, including the checkpoint record's `txId`, so a new transaction never reuses an id that is still in the log.

drill.title: Write recovery from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `recover()` for a store whose log has BEGIN, UPDATE (page, value), COMMIT, ABORT and CHECKPOINT (value = redo LSN) records, whose control file holds the last checkpoint record's LSN, and whose pages carry an `lsn`. Changes reach pages only at commit. Then answer: what makes running it twice safe?

recap: A commit appends records to the write-ahead log and forces it; the changed pages stay dirty in memory and are written later.
The commit rule: COMMIT returns only once the log is durable past the commit record. The WAL rule: a page is written only once the log is durable up to the page's LSN.
Every page carries the LSN of the last record that changed it. Recovery applies a record only to pages with an older LSN, so redo is idempotent.
A checkpoint flushes dirty pages and records a redo point, which `pg_control` points to; recovery starts there and ends at the first invalid record.
After a checkpoint, the first change to each page logs a full-page image, so a torn page can be restored. WAL volume jumps right after each checkpoint.
`synchronous_commit = off` can lose the last transactions but never half of one. `fsync = off` can corrupt the database.

quiz.q: A service runs with `synchronous_commit = off`, and the server loses power. What can happen to transactions whose COMMIT had already returned?
options: Nothing: COMMIT returned, so they are durable
The last few hundred milliseconds of them can be lost entirely, but none can be left half applied
Some of them can be half applied, so the database needs a manual check
All transactions since the last checkpoint are lost
quiz.why: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT returns before the log is flushed, and the WAL writer flushes within three times wal_writer_delay (600 ms by default). Those commits can vanish. The WAL rule still holds, so no page with their changes reached the disk ahead of their records, and nothing is half applied. Transactions flushed before the crash are recovered whether or not a checkpoint ran.

quiz.q: A buggy storage engine writes a dirty page to the data file without first flushing the log up to that page's LSN. The page holds the debit half of a committed-in-memory transfer whose COMMIT record was still in the log buffer. The power fails. What does recovery find?
options: The debit on disk and no record of the transfer in the log, so it can neither redo the credit nor undo the debit
Nothing wrong: recovery redoes the credit from the log
Nothing wrong: the checksum makes recovery discard the page
The transfer, complete, because pages are written in order
quiz.why: That is exactly what the WAL rule prevents. The log records describing the transfer were never made durable, so recovery has nothing to redo the credit from and nothing that says the debit should be removed. The page checksum is valid, since the page was written completely. The money is out of balance after a clean-looking recovery.

quiz.q: During recovery, a COMMIT record ends at LSN 0/4F00. The page it changed has page LSN 0/5000 on disk. What does redo do with that change?
options: Apply it, because committed changes are always redone
Stop recovery, because the page is newer than the log
Skip it: the page was written after a later change, so it already contains this one
Apply it and set the page LSN back to 0/4F00
quiz.why: A page LSN of 0/5000 means the page on disk already includes every change up to that point in the log, including this one. Applying an older change again could overwrite a newer value. Skipping is what makes redo idempotent. A page ahead of a record is normal; a page ahead of the end of the durable log would break the WAL rule.

quiz.q: Someone sets `full_page_writes = off` on a PostgreSQL server on ext4 to cut WAL volume. The power fails while an 8 KB page is being written. What is the risk?
options: None: the WAL has every change, so redo rebuilds the page
The page can be torn, half old and half new, and redo's small records can't repair it; data checksums can only report it
Only the last transaction is lost, as with synchronous_commit = off
The server refuses to start until full_page_writes is turned back on
quiz.why: Redo records describe small changes and assume the page they apply to is intact. A full-page image after each checkpoint gives recovery a whole copy to restore first. Without it, a torn page stays torn. Checksums (on by default for new clusters since PostgreSQL 18) detect the damage, they don't repair it. The docs allow turning it off only on file systems that prevent partial writes, such as ZFS.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: your LSM store acknowledges a put once it is in the memtable. What must it add so that an acknowledged put survives a crash, and when can that part of the log be deleted?
options: Nothing: SSTables are durable
Flush the memtable after every put
Append each put to a write-ahead log and force it before acknowledging (batching puts with group commit); delete that log once the memtable has been flushed to an SSTable
Keep a Bloom filter of acknowledged keys
quiz.why: The memtable is in RAM, so a crash loses it, as the lab test showed. Logging each put first and forcing the log makes it durable; on restart, replaying the log rebuilds the memtable. Once that memtable is written out as a forced SSTable, its log is no longer needed. Flushing the memtable on every put would make tiny SSTables and lose the point of an LSM tree.

flashcards.front: What does PostgreSQL write to disk at COMMIT?
flashcards.back: The WAL up to and including the commit record, forced with fsync. The changed data pages stay dirty in shared_buffers.
Before a dirty page is written to the data file, the log must be durable at least up to that page's LSN.

flashcards.front: What is a page LSN, and what is it for?
flashcards.back: The LSN just past the last log record that changed the page, stored in the page header. Redo applies a record only if the page's LSN is older, which makes redo idempotent.

flashcards.front: What does a checkpoint do, and where does recovery start?
flashcards.back: It writes all dirty pages, fsyncs them and logs a checkpoint record with a redo point. Recovery starts at the redo point of the latest checkpoint, found through global/pg_control.

flashcards.front: What is a full-page image, and when is one logged?
flashcards.back: A copy of a whole page in the WAL, logged with the first change to that page after each checkpoint, so recovery can restore a torn page.

flashcards.front: What are ARIES's three recovery passes?
flashcards.back: Analysis finds the losers and the pages that may be behind. Redo repeats history, committed or not. Undo rolls the losers back and logs each step as a compensation record.

flashcards.front: How does PostgreSQL handle a transaction that never committed, after a crash?
flashcards.back: Redo replays its changes too, then it counts as aborted because it has no commit record, and MVCC hides its row versions. There is no undo pass.

terms.plain: An append-only log of changes that is made durable before the changed pages are written.
Log sequence number: a byte position in the WAL, written in PostgreSQL as two hex numbers like 0/2F12D5D8.
The LSN just past the last log record that changed a page, stored in the page header.
Writing all dirty pages and logging a redo point, so recovery can start there.
Replaying log records onto pages after a crash, skipping changes a page already has.
A page that is partly old and partly new on disk because a crash interrupted its write.
A whole page copied into the WAL on its first change after a checkpoint.
Dirty pages may reach disk before commit (steal), and commit doesn't write pages (no-force).

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "PostgreSQL must write our ledger rows into the table file before COMMIT returns, otherwise a crash would lose them." Explain what really happens at COMMIT, and how the rows come back after a crash.
explain_back.answer: At COMMIT, PostgreSQL forces the write-ahead log, not the table file. Every change was already described by a small log record, and the commit record goes last; once the log is fsynced past it, COMMIT returns. The ledger pages stay dirty in shared_buffers and are written later by the background writer or a checkpoint, and never before the log covers them. If the server crashes first, recovery starts at the redo point of the last checkpoint and replays the log onto the pages, skipping any change a page already has, which it can tell from the LSN stored in each page. So the rows come back from the log. This is faster than writing pages at commit, because the log is one sequential stream that many commits share, while the table pages are scattered.

deeper.body:
**Checkpoints that don't stop the world.** A checkpoint that froze every change while it wrote gigabytes of dirty pages would stall the database for seconds. PostgreSQL notes the redo point when a checkpoint starts, then writes the dirty pages spread over 90% of the time until the next one (`checkpoint_completion_target` = 0.9) while new changes keep arriving. ARIES calls this a fuzzy checkpoint. The pages on disk never form one consistent snapshot, and they don't need to, because recovery replays from the redo point anyway and the page LSNs sort out the rest.

**SQLite's two modes.** By default SQLite copies original pages to a rollback journal, writes the database file, and commits by deleting the journal. In WAL mode, available since SQLite 3.7.0, a commit appends a commit record to a `-wal` file and does not touch the database file. A checkpoint copies pages back, automatically once the WAL reaches 1,000 pages.

**Commits in the same breath.** One fsync makes every byte before it durable, so PostgreSQL commits that arrive together share one flush. `commit_delay` (0 by default) makes a committing backend wait a few microseconds for others to join, when at least `commit_siblings` (5) other transactions are active. On fast NVMe drives it rarely helps.

**Replicas are WAL replay that never ends.** A PostgreSQL streaming replica receives the primary's WAL and runs the same redo code that crash recovery uses, forever. That is why a replica's pages are physically identical to the primary's, and why the Replication track can treat replication as shipping a log.
